claim: Adaptation is a fundamental property of cortical neurons.
source: Adaptation is a fundamental property of cortical neurons and has been suggested to be altered in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cortical neuron properties.

claim: Adaptation has been suggested to be altered in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
source: Adaptation is a fundamental property of cortical neurons and has been suggested to be altered in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
evidence: This refers to prior research suggestions in the literature.

claim: Initial transient fMRI responses to audio-visual stimulation were equivalent between ASD and NT groups in both visual and auditory cortices.
source: The initial transient responses were equivalent between groups in both visual and auditory cortices and when stimulation occurred with fixed-interval and randomized-interval timing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Initial transient fMRI responses were equivalent between ASD and NT groups when stimulation occurred with fixed-interval timing.
source: The initial transient responses were equivalent between groups in both visual and auditory cortices and when stimulation occurred with fixed-interval and randomized-interval timing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Initial transient fMRI responses were equivalent between ASD and NT groups when stimulation occurred with randomized-interval timing.
source: The initial transient responses were equivalent between groups in both visual and auditory cortices and when stimulation occurred with fixed-interval and randomized-interval timing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: In auditory cortex, the post-transient sustained response was greater in individuals with ASD than NT controls in the fixed-interval timing condition.
source: However, in auditory but not visual cortex, the post-transient sustained response was greater in individuals with ASD than NT controls in the fixed-interval timing condition, reflecting reduced adaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: In visual cortex, the post-transient sustained response was not greater in individuals with ASD than NT controls in the fixed-interval timing condition.
source: However, in auditory but not visual cortex, the post-transient sustained response was greater in individuals with ASD than NT controls in the fixed-interval timing condition, reflecting reduced adaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The greater sustained response in auditory cortex in ASD compared to NT reflects reduced adaptation.
source: However, in auditory but not visual cortex, the post-transient sustained response was greater in individuals with ASD than NT controls in the fixed-interval timing condition, reflecting reduced adaptation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the understanding of adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Individual differences in the sustained response in auditory cortex correlated with ASD symptom severity.
source: Further, individual differences in the sustained response in auditory cortex correlated with ASD symptom severity.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis between fMRI data and ADOS scores.

claim: ASD is associated with increased neural responsiveness.
source: These findings are consistent with hypotheses that ASD is associated with increased neural responsiveness but that responsiveness differences only manifest after repeated stimulation, are specific to the temporal pattern of stimulation, and are confined to specific cortical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings in the context of existing hypotheses.

claim: Responsiveness differences in ASD only manifest after repeated stimulation.
source: These findings are consistent with hypotheses that ASD is associated with increased neural responsiveness but that responsiveness differences only manifest after repeated stimulation, are specific to the temporal pattern of stimulation, and are confined to specific cortical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings showing differences in sustained but not transient responses.

claim: Responsiveness differences in ASD are specific to the temporal pattern of stimulation.
source: These findings are consistent with hypotheses that ASD is associated with increased neural responsiveness but that responsiveness differences only manifest after repeated stimulation, are specific to the temporal pattern of stimulation, and are confined to specific cortical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings showing differences in fixed-interval but not randomized-interval conditions.

claim: Responsiveness differences in ASD are confined to specific cortical regions.
source: These findings are consistent with hypotheses that ASD is associated with increased neural responsiveness but that responsiveness differences only manifest after repeated stimulation, are specific to the temporal pattern of stimulation, and are confined to specific cortical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings showing differences in auditory but not visual cortex.

claim: A unifying theme of numerous proposals is that the pathophysiology of autism is related to a pervasive increase in neural responsiveness.
source: However, a unifying theme of numerous proposals is that the pathophysiology of autism is related to a pervasive increase in neural responsiveness (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Markram and Markram, 2010; Gogolla et al., 2009; Blatt and Fatemi, 2011; Gatto and Broadie, 2010; Pizzarelli and Cherubini, 2011; Yizhar et al., 2011; Hussman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Outside of cases in specific animal models of autism, experimental evidence for increased neural responses has been limited.
source: However, outside of cases in specific animal models of autism (Bateup et al., 2011; Contractor et al., 2015; Bateup et al., 2013), experimental evidence for increased neural responses has been limited.
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal model studies and the general state of the literature.

claim: Studies in humans across a variety of brain regions and measurement techniques have yielded equivocal results regarding neural responses in ASD.
source: Studies in humans across a variety of brain regions and measurement techniques have yielded equivocal results, with recent studies finding equivalent (Dinstein et al., 2012), or even decreased (Haigh et al., 2015) neural responses in subjects with ASDs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claim: Recent studies have found equivalent neural responses in subjects with ASDs.
source: Studies in humans across a variety of brain regions and measurement techniques have yielded equivocal results, with recent studies finding equivalent (Dinstein et al., 2012), or even decreased (Haigh et al., 2015) neural responses in subjects with ASDs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dinstein et al., 2012.

claim: Recent studies have found decreased neural responses in subjects with ASDs.
source: Studies in humans across a variety of brain regions and measurement techniques have yielded equivocal results, with recent studies finding equivalent (Dinstein et al., 2012), or even decreased (Haigh et al., 2015) neural responses in subjects with ASDs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haigh et al., 2015.

claim: Behavioral observations show reduced adaptation in ASD in tactile stimulation.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by behavioral observations of reduced adaptation in ASD across diverse domains, including tactile stimulation (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014), face discrimination (Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012), gaze direction (Pellicano et al., 2013), numerosity (Turi et al., 2015), audio-visual asynchrony (Noel et al., 2017), and saccade amplitude (Mosconi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral observations show reduced adaptation in ASD in face discrimination.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by behavioral observations of reduced adaptation in ASD across diverse domains, including tactile stimulation (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014), face discrimination (Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012), gaze direction (Pellicano et al., 2013), numerosity (Turi et al., 2015), audio-visual asynchrony (Noel et al., 2017), and saccade amplitude (Mosconi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral observations show reduced adaptation in ASD in gaze direction.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by behavioral observations of reduced adaptation in ASD across diverse domains, including tactile stimulation (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014), face discrimination (Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012), gaze direction (Pellicano et al., 2013), numerosity (Turi et al., 2015), audio-visual asynchrony (Noel et al., 2017), and saccade amplitude (Mosconi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral observations show reduced adaptation in ASD in numerosity.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by behavioral observations of reduced adaptation in ASD across diverse domains, including tactile stimulation (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014), face discrimination (Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012), gaze direction (Pellicano et al., 2013), numerosity (Turi et al., 2015), audio-visual asynchrony (Noel et al., 2017), and saccade amplitude (Mosconi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral observations show reduced adaptation in ASD in audio-visual asynchrony.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by behavioral observations of reduced adaptation in ASD across diverse domains, including tactile stimulation (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014), face discrimination (Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012), gaze direction (Pellicano et al., 2013), numerosity (Turi et al., 2015), audio-visual asynchrony (Noel et al., 2017), and saccade amplitude (Mosconi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral observations show reduced adaptation in ASD in saccade amplitude.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by behavioral observations of reduced adaptation in ASD across diverse domains, including tactile stimulation (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014), face discrimination (Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012), gaze direction (Pellicano et al., 2013), numerosity (Turi et al., 2015), audio-visual asynchrony (Noel et al., 2017), and saccade amplitude (Mosconi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Theoretical work has suggested that many of the core symptoms of ASD can be framed as an inability to form predictions.
source: Further, theoretical work has suggested that many of the core symptoms of ASD, including the failure to adapt or habituate, can be framed as an inability to form predictions (Sinha et al., 2014) and incorporate prior experiences (Pellicano and Burr, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sinha et al., 2014.

claim: Theoretical work has suggested that many of the core symptoms of ASD can be framed as an inability to incorporate prior experiences.
source: Further, theoretical work has suggested that many of the core symptoms of ASD, including the failure to adapt or habituate, can be framed as an inability to form predictions (Sinha et al., 2014) and incorporate prior experiences (Pellicano and Burr, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pellicano and Burr, 2012.

claim: The specificity of sensory symptoms that occur in individuals with ASD suggests that adaptation differences may be modality specific and confined to particular regions of cortex.
source: Finally, the specificity of sensory symptoms that occur in individuals with ASD (Leekam et al., 2007; Brown and Dunn, 2002) suggests that adaptation differences may be modality specific and confined to particular regions of cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited observations about sensory symptoms in ASD.

claim: Reaction times (RTs) in response to the first stimulus presentation of a block were equivalent for ASD and NT participants.
source: Reaction times (RTs) in response to the first stimulus presentation of a block were equivalent for ASD and NT participants (group x timing condition ANOVA; F1,46 = 0.26, p=0.61; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis with statistical support.

claim: RTs for all other trials (2-10) were shorter for the ASD participants.
source: RTs for all other trials were shorter for the ASD participants; using the mean RT over trials 2 – 10 there was a significant main effect of group (F1,46 = 4.84, p=0.03), a main effect of timing condition (F1,1 = 58.9, p<0.001), and no interaction (F1,46 = 0.002; p=0.97).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis with statistical support.

claim: There was no group difference in response errors defined by more than one button press per trial.
source: There was no group difference in response errors defined by more than one button press per trial (F1,46 = 0.71, p=0.13).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis with statistical support.

claim: In the auditory ROI, there was a significant main effect of group (ASD and NT) on sustained response.
source: In the auditory ROI, there was a significant main effect of group (ASD and NT; F1,38 = 8.69, p=0.005), a trend of timing conditions (fixed- and randomized-interval; F1,1 = 3.51, p<0.07), and no interaction between the two (F1,38 = 0.295, p=0.59).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: In the auditory ROI, there was a trend of timing conditions (fixed- and randomized-interval) on sustained response.
source: In the auditory ROI, there was a significant main effect of group (ASD and NT; F1,38 = 8.69, p=0.005), a trend of timing conditions (fixed- and randomized-interval; F1,1 = 3.51, p<0.07), and no interaction between the two (F1,38 = 0.295, p=0.59).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: In the auditory ROI, there was no interaction between group and timing condition on sustained response.
source: In the auditory ROI, there was a significant main effect of group (ASD and NT; F1,38 = 8.69, p=0.005), a trend of timing conditions (fixed- and randomized-interval; F1,1 = 3.51, p<0.07), and no interaction between the two (F1,38 = 0.295, p=0.59).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: There was a significant difference between NT and ASD in the auditory ROI sustained response in the fixed-interval condition.
source: Planned comparisons showed that there was only a significant difference between NT and ASD in the fixed-interval condition (t38 = 2.46, p=0.02, Cohen's d = 0.79) and not in the randomized-interval condition (t38 = 1.58, p=0.12, Cohen's d = 0.50).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: There was no significant difference between NT and ASD in the auditory ROI sustained response in the randomized-interval condition.
source: Planned comparisons showed that there was only a significant difference between NT and ASD in the fixed-interval condition (t38 = 2.46, p=0.02, Cohen's d = 0.79) and not in the randomized-interval condition (t38 = 1.58, p=0.12, Cohen's d = 0.50).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: In the visual ROI, there were no significant main effects of group or timing condition on sustained response.
source: In the visual ROI, there were no significant main effects (group, F1,42 = 1.07, p=0.31; timing condition, F1,1 = 2.44, p=0.13) or interactions (F1,42 = 0.16, p=0.69) in the sustained response.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: In the visual ROI, there were no significant interactions between group and timing condition on sustained response.
source: In the visual ROI, there were no significant main effects (group, F1,42 = 1.07, p=0.31; timing condition, F1,1 = 2.44, p=0.13) or interactions (F1,42 = 0.16, p=0.69) in the sustained response.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis with statistical support.

claim: Sustained response in the auditory ROI during the fixed-interval condition was significantly correlated with ADOS scores.
source: Sustained response in the auditory ROI during the fixed-interval condition was significantly correlated with ADOS scores (r = 0.53; p=0.02; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: Correlations between ADOS scores and the sustained response in the randomized-interval condition were not statistically significant.
source: Correlations between ADOS scores and the sustained response in the randomized-interval condition (r = 0.07; p=0.78) and with both timing conditions in the visual ROI (fixed-interval, r = 0.28, p=0.24; randomized-interval, r = 0.06, p=0.81) were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: Correlations between ADOS scores and the sustained response in the visual ROI in both timing conditions were not statistically significant.
source: Correlations between ADOS scores and the sustained response in the randomized-interval condition (r = 0.07; p=0.78) and with both timing conditions in the visual ROI (fixed-interval, r = 0.28, p=0.24; randomized-interval, r = 0.06, p=0.81) were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: The fMRI signal 'undershoot' during the post-stimulus period was lower in NT compared to ASD individuals.
source: In addition to the sustained response difference between ASD and NT in auditory cortex, we also observed that the fMRI signal 'undershoot' during the post-stimulus period (i.e. during the blank period after the 20 s stimulus block was over) was lower in NT compared to ASD individuals (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data.

claim: The difference in sustained response in auditory cortex remained in the fixed-interval condition when groups were matched for post-stimulus response magnitude.
source: Comparing these matched groups, we found that the difference in sustained response in auditory cortex remained in the fixed-interval condition (Figure 4; t23 = 1.99, p=0.058).
evidence: This is a finding from the matched-groups analysis with statistical support.

claim: Any mechanism that creates a post-stimulus difference, by itself, is not sufficient to also cause a difference in sustained response.
source: We also note that the largest post-stimulus difference is in visual cortex and, despite the large difference, the sustained response is equivalent in both groups. Thus, any mechanism that creates a post-stimulus difference, by itself, is not sufficient to also cause a difference in sustained response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that visual cortex shows post-stimulus differences but no sustained response differences.

claim: AASP responses showed a pattern consistent with low auditory threshold for ASD vs. NT individuals.
source: Consistent with our prediction AASP responses showed a pattern consistent with low auditory threshold for ASD vs. NT individuals (i.e. higher responses on questions associated with sensory sensitivity or sensory avoiding; t78 = 3.14, p=0.002, Cohen's d = 0.70).
evidence: This is a finding from the AASP questionnaire analysis with statistical support.

claim: There were no significant group differences in AASP scores associated with a high threshold in the auditory domain.
source: There were no significant group differences in scores associated with a high threshold in the auditory domain (t78 = 0.86, p=0.40, Cohen's d = 0.19) or either a low (t78 = 1.56, p=0.12, Cohen's d = 0.34) or high (t78 = 1.11, p=0.27, Cohen's d = 0.25) threshold in the visual domain.
evidence: This is a finding from the AASP questionnaire analysis with statistical support.

claim: There were no significant group differences in AASP scores associated with a low threshold in the visual domain.
source: There were no significant group differences in scores associated with a high threshold in the auditory domain (t78 = 0.86, p=0.40, Cohen's d = 0.19) or either a low (t78 = 1.56, p=0.12, Cohen's d = 0.34) or high (t78 = 1.11, p=0.27, Cohen's d = 0.25) threshold in the visual domain.
evidence: This is a finding from the AASP questionnaire analysis with statistical support.

claim: There were no significant group differences in AASP scores associated with a high threshold in the visual domain.
source: There were no significant group differences in scores associated with a high threshold in the auditory domain (t78 = 0.86, p=0.40, Cohen's d = 0.19) or either a low (t78 = 1.56, p=0.12, Cohen's d = 0.34) or high (t78 = 1.11, p=0.27, Cohen's d = 0.25) threshold in the visual domain.
evidence: This is a finding from the AASP questionnaire analysis with statistical support.

claim: There were no significant statistical relationships between individual differences in the auditory- and visual-specific sensory processing scores and individual differences in the fMRI sustained response.
source: Although consistent with our prediction, the generalizability of the AASP results should be interpreted with some caution; there were no significant statistical relationships between individual differences in the auditory- and visual-specific sensory processing scores and individual differences in the fMRI sustained response.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: When limiting the sample to subjects that participated in the fMRI experiment the group difference in low sensory auditory threshold did not reach statistical significance.
source: And when limiting the sample to subjects that participated in the fMRI experiment the group difference in low sensory auditory threshold did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This is a finding from the AASP questionnaire analysis with a restricted sample.

claim: Both the fMRI and behavioral questionnaire findings are consistent with a hypothesis that auditory sensory processing may be more disrupted in individuals with ASD compared to visual sensory processing.
source: However, overall, both the fMRI and behavioral questionnaire findings are consistent with a hypothesis that auditory sensory processing may be more disrupted in individuals with ASD compared to visual sensory processing and reflect elevated neural responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined fMRI and AASP findings.

claim: The most likely interpretation for the results is that there is reduced auditory adaptation in individuals with ASD compared to NT controls.
source: The most likely interpretation for these results is that there is reduced auditory adaptation in individuals with ASD compared to NT controls.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: Adaptation is a neural regulatory process that adjusts neural responses to the current sensory environment.
source: Adaptation is a neural regulatory process that adjusts neural responses to the current sensory environment and, with very simple stimulus conditions such as those in our experiment, often involves response reductions (Kohn, 2007; Solomon and Kohn, 2014; Larsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: With very simple stimulus conditions, adaptation often involves response reductions.
source: Adaptation is a neural regulatory process that adjusts neural responses to the current sensory environment and, with very simple stimulus conditions such as those in our experiment, often involves response reductions (Kohn, 2007; Solomon and Kohn, 2014; Larsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Auditory cortex is highly sensitive to stimulus temporal structure.
source: In auditory cortex, a region that is highly sensitive to stimulus temporal structure (Boemio et al., 2005), neural adaptation is more likely when the temporal structure of the stimulation occurs at regular intervals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In auditory cortex, neural adaptation is more likely when the temporal structure of the stimulation occurs at regular intervals.
source: In auditory cortex, a region that is highly sensitive to stimulus temporal structure (Boemio et al., 2005), neural adaptation is more likely when the temporal structure of the stimulation occurs at regular intervals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of auditory cortex and general adaptation principles.

claim: Auditory adaptation in response to repeated sounds is larger for expected versus unexpected stimuli.
source: For example, auditory adaptation in response to repeated sounds is larger for expected versus unexpected stimuli (Todorovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Todorovic et al., 2011.

claim: In NTs, a representation of the regular temporal structure in the fixed-interval timing condition is formed after approximately 3–4 stimulus presentations.
source: We suggest that in NTs, a representation of the regular temporal structure in the fixed-interval timing condition is formed after approximately 3–4 stimulus presentations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of when sustained response differences emerge.

claim: The representation of regular temporal structure leads to a reduction in responses to subsequent stimulus presentations in NTs.
source: This representation leads to a reduction in responses to subsequent stimulus presentations.
evidence: This is an inference based on adaptation mechanisms.

claim: In ASD, either a representation of the fixed stimulus timing was not as strongly formed, or the representation does not subsequently influence neural responses as strongly.
source: In ASD, either a representation of the fixed stimulus timing was not as strongly formed, or the representation does not subsequently influence neural responses as strongly.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: The neural response in individuals with ASD reflects an inability to extract the temporal regularities of the stimulation sequence.
source: That the neural response in individuals with ASD reflects an inability to extract the temporal regularities of the stimulation sequence is consistent with theoretical accounts that suggest that many of the core symptoms of ASD, including the failure to adapt or habituate, can be framed as an inability to form predictions (Sinha et al., 2014) and incorporate prior experiences (Pellicano and Burr, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical accounts supported by citations.

claim: In the randomized interval condition where there was no temporal regularity in the stimulation, no significant differences emerged between ASD and NT participants.
source: Further supporting this interpretation, in the randomized interval condition where there was no temporal regularity in the stimulation, no significant differences emerged between ASD and NT participants and there was no relationship between the sustained response and ASD symptom severity.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: In the randomized interval condition, there was no relationship between the sustained response and ASD symptom severity.
source: Further supporting this interpretation, in the randomized interval condition where there was no temporal regularity in the stimulation, no significant differences emerged between ASD and NT participants and there was no relationship between the sustained response and ASD symptom severity.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: A simple model of adaptation where neural response magnitudes for each stimulus presentation in a fixed-interval block begins to reduce after the second stimulus presentation and asymptotes after the fifth stimulus presentation can explain the observed fMRI timecourses.
source: We implemented a simple model of adaptation where neural response magnitudes for each stimulus presentation in a fixed-interval block begins to reduce after the second stimulus presentation and asymptotes after the fifth stimulus presentation. ASD and NT model responses only differed in their asymptotic response magnitude (lower for NT than ASD). Convolving these different modeled neural responses with a canonical hemodynamic response function yields a predicted fMRI timecourse that closely resembles our auditory cortex measurements for ASD and NT participants (Figure 5), suggesting at least one plausible way in which underlying neural responses might differ between ASD and NT over the course of successive stimulus presentations.
evidence: This is a modeling result that provides a plausible mechanistic explanation.

claim: Previous findings that have assessed adaptation in ASD using physiological measures such as electrodermal and respiratory/pulse-rate yielded no definitive conclusion about whether habituation was altered in ASD.
source: Older findings that relied on physiological measures such as electrodermal (van Engeland, 1984) and respiratory/pulse-rate (James and Barry, 1980), yielded no definitive conclusion about whether habituation was altered in ASD (Rogers and Ozonoff, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and reviews.

claim: More recent findings using behavioral measures across a broad range of stimulus types and paradigms have demonstrated more consistent evidence of reduced adaptation in ASD.
source: However, more recent findings using behavioral measures across a broad range of stimulus types and paradigms (Tommerdahl et al., 2007; Tannan et al., 2008; Puts et al., 2014; Pellicano et al., 2007; Fiorentini et al., 2012; Pellicano et al., 2013; Turi et al., 2015; Noel et al., 2017; Mosconi et al., 2013) have demonstrated more consistent evidence of reduced adaptation in ASD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Recent brain imaging results have shown that subjects with ASD show less reduction in fMRI response than NT subjects to aversive stimulation, measured in successive blocks of presentation.
source: In addition, recent brain imaging results have shown that subjects with ASD show less reduction in fMRI response than NT subjects to aversive stimulation, measured in successive blocks of presentation (Green et al., 2015), however, without a manipulation of stimulus properties it is unclear whether this effect reflects neural or hemodynamic properties or whether it relies on the same processes as the rapidly appearing differences observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Green et al., 2015.

claim: fMRI adaptation paradigms using face stimuli have shown reduced adaptation/habituation in regions such as the amygdala in ASD.
source: In addition, fMRI adaptation paradigms using face stimuli have shown reduced adaptation/habituation in regions such as the amygdala (Kleinhans et al., 2009) and fusiform face area (Ewbank et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: fMRI adaptation paradigms using face stimuli have shown reduced adaptation/habituation in the fusiform face area in ASD.
source: In addition, fMRI adaptation paradigms using face stimuli have shown reduced adaptation/habituation in regions such as the amygdala (Kleinhans et al., 2009) and fusiform face area (Ewbank et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: The results reveal an early sensory disruption of adaptation to non-social stimuli.
source: In contrast, our results reveal an early sensory disruption of adaptation to non-social stimuli and are consistent with previous ERP findings of reduced habituation to repeated sounds in infants at high risk for autism (BASIS Team et al., 2011.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings.

claim: The results are consistent with previous ERP findings of reduced habituation to repeated sounds in infants at high risk for autism.
source: In contrast, our results reveal an early sensory disruption of adaptation to non-social stimuli and are consistent with previous ERP findings of reduced habituation to repeated sounds in infants at high risk for autism (BASIS Team et al., 2011.
evidence: This is supported by citation to BASIS Team et al., 2011.

claim: A recent investigation revealed equivalent fMRI repetition suppression in the visual system in individuals with ASD.
source: Indeed, a recent investigation revealed equivalent fMRI repetition suppression in the visual system in individuals with ASD (Utzerath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Utzerath et al., 2018.

claim: The contributions of different mechanisms that underlie adaptation may vary by cortical region.
source: However, the contributions of different mechanisms that underlie adaptation (Lanting et al., 2013) may vary by cortical region.
evidence: This is speculation based on cited knowledge about adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Future research that uses timing and/or stimulus parameters that are more specifically tailored to properties of early visual cortical neurons may reveal differences in early sensory adaptation between ASD and NT individuals.
source: It is possible that future research that uses timing and/or stimulus parameters that are more specifically tailored to properties of early visual cortical neurons (Fang et al., 2005) may reveal differences in early sensory adaptation between ASD and NT individuals.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: Previous findings have suggested there may be disrupted audio-visual integration in individuals with ASD.
source: Further, our procedure used a combined auditory-visual stimulus and previous findings have suggested there may be disrupted audio-visual integration in individuals with ASD (Foss-Feig et al., 2010; Kwakye et al., 2011; Stevenson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: ASD participants responded with shorter RTs and there was no obvious speed-accuracy tradeoff.
source: ASD participants responded with shorter RTs and there was no obvious speed-accuracy (i.e. pressing the button more) tradeoff.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Recent meta-analyses demonstrate no difference in RT between ASD participants and controls.
source: This result is surprising given recent meta-analyses demonstrating no difference in RT between ASD participants and controls (Ferraro, 2016), a conclusion consistent with our observation of no RT differences for first-trials in a block.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferraro, 2016.

claim: Motor-related signals can suppress excitatory neurons in auditory cortex.
source: With respect to our fMRI findings, it is known that motor-related signals can suppress excitatory neurons in auditory cortex (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sensory symptoms are now included in the diagnostic criteria for ASD.
source: Sensory symptoms, now included in the diagnostic criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), are very common in ASD (Leekam et al., 2007; Brown and Dunn, 2002; Rogers and Ozonoff, 2005; Ben-Sasson et al., 2009) and persist across age (Leekam et al., 2007), are present in all cognitive abilities (Leekam et al., 2007), and have unique features when compared to other neurodevelopmental disorders (Rogers et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DSM-5.

claim: Sensory symptoms are very common in ASD.
source: Sensory symptoms, now included in the diagnostic criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), are very common in ASD (Leekam et al., 2007; Brown and Dunn, 2002; Rogers and Ozonoff, 2005; Ben-Sasson et al., 2009) and persist across age (Leekam et al., 2007), are present in all cognitive abilities (Leekam et al., 2007), and have unique features when compared to other neurodevelopmental disorders (Rogers et al., 2003).

claim: Sensory symptoms in ASD persist across age.
